I'm 75/25 on the idea of government intervention/regulation of social media.

First of all, mostly as an aside, almost all countries except the US have forced government intervention on social media, and arrests made based on social media posts.

But I'd say that if social media claims to be a service they should not be allowed to censor free speech any more than the government should be able to. They are not publishing houses. Putt does not look through every Voat comment and decide what should and should not be posted. They are autonomous services, who increasingly are hiding behind this shield of removing what they claim is "false or misleading information" (inevitably they decide what is false/misleading) or "hate speech". It's no longer their platform, though. It's the platform of all users who create content. Without content creators, YouTube would be nothing.

I would say there are exactly 3 categories of stuff which should be removed, and these categories should be applied as narrowly (in the legal sense) as possible:

  • Illegal content. Child pornography. /r/darknetmarkets
  • Phishing sites. Fake login pages for actual websites.
  • Spam. Actually trying to sell something. Political speech is not spam. Repetitive content is not spam.

I would argue that (2) and (3) are actually very minor problems, and sites can and do exist that allow anonymous posts of all content, that aren't flooded by spam. A legal requirement for social media would be similar to net neutrality. Websites which desire to do business in the US which allow automated posting of user content may not remove that content except under the circumstances defined above. That does not apply in the case of active moderation. If you have a human review the comments for your site and approve each one instead of posting-then-deleting, the law no longer applies. For example, sites that cater to children may wish to use that.
